title: The 1973 Crash Nobody Remembers
note: 1973 crash vs 2026 parallels; timelines + overlay charts.

scenes.narration: You remember the famous ones. 1929. The dot-com bust. 2008. The crashes that got documentaries and movies.
But there's one enormous crash that almost nobody talks about anymore — and it might be the most important one for right now.
If you've ever been told to just buy stocks and hold for the long run, and you'll always come out ahead — this is the giant asterisk on that advice.
In 1973 and '74, the U.S. stock market lost nearly half of its entire value.
Nearly half the market, just gone. And yet that isn't even the scary part.
Here's the scary part. In real, inflation-adjusted terms, it took about twenty years to recover.
scenes.sub: to get your money back — in real terms

scenes.narration: A dollar invested at the 1973 top didn't fully recover its buying power until the 1990s. That's an entire investing lifetime, erased.
We're taught crashes are loud — a chaotic trading floor, a red screen, a panicked headline. 1973 was the exact opposite.
It was so slow and so quiet that most people didn't even realize they were living through one of the worst bear markets in history.
So two questions. Why does nobody remember this one? And why does 2026 look so eerily like 1973?
Because this isn't a history lesson. It's a mirror. Four things that broke the market in 1973 are all back, right now.
So let's put the two eras side by side, and follow the money all the way down.
scenes.heading: The 1973 Crash Nobody Remembers

scenes.narration: First, how 1973 actually came apart — step by step.
scenes.title: How 1973 came apart

scenes.narration: Rhyme one: the glamour stocks. In the early seventies, investors crowded into a handful of 'can't-lose' companies.
They were called the Nifty Fifty. 'One-decision stocks' — you decide once to buy, and you simply never sell.
The quality felt so obvious that the price was treated as irrelevant. Pay anything — they'll always go up.
And these really were great companies — it's all documented. The mistake was believing no price was ever too high.
At the peak, the Nifty Fifty traded at forty-two times earnings — more than double the rest of the market.
Polaroid alone traded at ninety-one times earnings. For a camera company. The business was real; the price was fantasy.
Then gravity showed up. From their highs, Polaroid fell ninety-one percent. Avon, eighty-six. Xerox, seventy-one.
Now swap the names and keep the setup. Does this look familiar?
Because today, seven companies make up around a third of the entire S&P 500 — a concentration we haven't seen since… you guessed it.
And to be clear: the Magnificent Seven are phenomenal businesses. So were the Nifty Fifty. That was never the question.
Sound crazy? It's the exact logic you hear today. 'Just buy the best companies and hold forever — valuation doesn't matter.'
To translate forty-two times earnings: you were paying forty-two dollars for every one dollar the company made in a year.
At that price, the business has to grow flawlessly for years just for you to break even. One stumble, and the stock craters.
And here's the gut-punch: many of those companies kept growing just fine. The businesses were healthy. The stocks still got cut in half.
When a handful of names carry the whole index, your 'diversified' fund quietly becomes a concentrated bet on just a few companies.
And it really is a tiny club — seven companies that have quietly grown to dominate the entire index.
In 1972 that same bet looked unbeatable. By 1974, the glamour stocks had dragged the entire market down with them.
That's the hidden danger of concentration. When the giants fall, there's nothing left to hold the index up.
And the feeling driving it is the same in every era. Everyone's getting rich but you. So you buy — at the top, for the most money, with the least caution.
The four most expensive words in investing are, reliably, 'this time is different.' In 1972, they cost people half their savings.
To understand that inflation, rewind to 1971. Nixon cut the dollar's last tie to gold — and money could now be printed far more freely.
Rhyme two: the inflation shock. In 1973, inflation arrived in a form you could see from your car window.
OPEC cut off the oil. The price quadrupled almost overnight, and gas lines stretched around the block.
This is the embargo that lit the fuse — a geopolitical shock that slammed straight into everyday prices.
And inflation didn't just tick up. It exploded into double digits — north of twelve percent.
2022 had a totally different trigger — a pandemic, a war — but the exact same result: the worst inflation in forty years.
And once it starts, it feeds itself. Prices rise, so workers demand raises, so costs rise, so prices rise again — a spiral that's brutal to stop.
Different decade. Different cause. The exact same fever chart.
scenes.title: Inflation rate (%)

scenes.narration: And that's not me massaging the numbers — here's the Fed's own inflation data, with the 1970s spike and the 2020s spike on one chart.
And just like the seventies, the people in charge first reassured everyone it was 'transitory.' It was not.
Prices for everything — food, rent, gas — climbed faster than paychecks. Your money quietly shrank while you held it.
Two totally different sparks — an oil embargo, then a pandemic — lighting the exact same fire. That's the rhyme.
And inflation doesn't just hurt stocks. It torches bonds too — because a fixed payment is worth less when every dollar buys less.
That's the seventies nightmare: stocks AND bonds falling together. The one place everyone hides had no exits.
It happened again in 2022 — the classic safe portfolio had one of its worst years in a century.
Rhyme three: the Fed slams the brakes. To strangle 1970s inflation, the Fed cranked interest rates to brutal highs.
Look familiar? Here are Fed interest rates across both eras — a wall of hikes in the seventies, and another wall just now.
And here's the chain that actually breaks markets: high inflation forces high rates — and high rates crush the price of everything.
Because when money stops being free, the most expensive stocks fall the hardest. In 1973, that was the Nifty Fifty.
In the seventies it took a legendary Fed chair, Paul Volcker, to finally break inflation — by hiking rates to nearly twenty percent.

scenes.label: PAUL VOLCKER
scenes.caption: the Fed chair who broke inflation
scenes.narration: That's him — Paul Volcker. The blunt, cigar-chewing Fed chair who was willing to trigger a recession to kill inflation for good.
That cure triggered a brutal recession. Killing inflation is never free — someone always ends up paying the bill.
Cheap money had inflated the glamour stocks for years. Expensive money is exactly what finally popped them.
And rate hikes work on a delay. Economists call them 'long and variable lags' — the pain shows up months, even years, later.
Which is why a calm market today proves nothing. In 1973, the worst of the damage came well after the headlines moved on.
Right now the hope is a 'soft landing' — inflation cools, nobody gets hurt. It's possible. It's also exactly what everyone hoped for in 1973.
Rhyme four: the ground underneath. Stagflation — a stalling economy and rising prices at the same time.
The textbooks said that combination couldn't even happen. In the seventies, it happened for a decade.
It's a real, named thing — and it's exactly the corner an economy gets stuck in when prices rise but growth doesn't.
And sitting on top of all of it, one number: how expensive stocks are versus a decade of real earnings. The CAPE ratio.
In 1966 it hit twenty-four — and then came a long, grinding bear market. Today it sits around forty.
scenes.title: Shiller CAPE ratio

scenes.narration: This one's live — the Shiller P/E today, near forty, a level beaten only once in history: the peak of the dot-com bubble.
And history is blunt about what that tends to mean. From valuations this high, the next decade of market returns has usually been weak — low single digits, sometimes nothing.
The bulls say it's justified now — lower rates, fatter profits, buybacks. Maybe. But that's the same reassurance offered at every single top.
High valuations don't cause a crash by themselves. But they're the dry wood. 1973 had a forest of it. So does 2026.
Think of a high CAPE as a smoke detector, not a stopwatch. It can't tell you WHEN. It can tell you the room is full of gas.
Here's why it matters. Historically, the higher the CAPE on the day you buy, the lower your returns over the next decade.
And every bubble sings the same anthem: 'this time is different' — because of railroads, radio, dot-coms, and now AI.
Sometimes it genuinely is a little different. It's just never different enough to make a crazy price safe.
And CAPE isn't some fringe idea — it's the measure a Nobel-winning economist built specifically to spot exactly this.
There's a second gauge that agrees: the total value of the stock market versus the whole economy. It's also near record highs.
And today's anthem is the AI boom — just as the 1960s had the 'go-go' tech of its day. Massive spending, sky-high hopes.
Put the four rhymes side by side, and the picture gets uncomfortable.
Glamour-stock mania. An inflation shock. A Fed slamming the brakes. And valuations near all-time highs. 1973 had all four. We have all four.
This is not a prediction. Nobody can time a market, and anyone who says they can is selling something.
It's a pattern. And patterns, in markets, are worth respecting — especially the ones everyone's decided to forget.
And to be fair to the other side: a setup can simmer for years before anything breaks. Being early can feel exactly like being wrong.
The market can absolutely climb higher from here. The 1972 market did too — for months — right before it didn't.
So why has 1973 vanished from memory, when 1929 and 2008 are practically legends?
Because it didn't crash in a single day. There was no Black Tuesday, no one unforgettable photo. It was a slow, grinding, two-year bleed.
No cliff to gasp at. Just a long, relentless slide — the kind that's easy to look away from.
scenes.title: S&P 500 · 1973–74

scenes.narration: The full record is right here — a forty-eight percent fall that took nearly two years to grind all the way down.
And then the second trick: inflation hid the wound. On paper, prices clawed back to 1973 levels by 1980.
But a 1980 dollar bought far less than a 1973 one. In real, spendable terms, investors waited until the 1990s to be whole.
This is the trap in one line: the nominal number lies to you, and only the real, inflation-adjusted number tells the truth.
So the chart 'recovered.' Your actual buying power did not. For twenty years, you were poorer and the headline never said so.
That's the kind nobody puts in a movie. The quiet crash — the one inflation quietly covers up.
Compare that to 2008 — a sudden, screaming panic packed into a few weeks. That's the kind of crash the brain files away and never forgets.
A slow bleed never trips that alarm. You adapt. You hope. You keep telling yourself it'll bounce back next quarter.
Japan learned the same lesson the hard way. Its 1989 market peak still hasn't fully recovered — decades later.
Even the U.S. had a quieter echo. From 2000 to roughly 2013, the market round-tripped to nowhere — a lost decade hiding in plain sight.
So the comforting line that 'stocks always go up over the long run' comes with a giant asterisk: it can depend entirely on the price you paid to get in.
Which is the real lesson here, and it's bigger than 1973. The dangerous crash isn't the loud one. It's the quiet one you don't notice for years.
scenes.bubble: The quiet crash is the dangerous one.

scenes.narration: And the Nifty Fifty taught the oldest rule in investing: a wonderful company, bought at a terrible price, is still a terrible investment.
Price is what you pay. Value is what you get. Pay ninety times earnings, and even a great company can take decades to pay you back.
So the Magnificent Seven can absolutely keep changing the world. Their stocks can still fall in half while they do it. Both things can be true.
So this isn't a reason to panic or dump everything. Trying to time the top is a loser's game in both directions.
It's a reason to respect price. To ask not just 'is this a great company' but 'is this a great company at THIS price.'
Spread your bets. Keep a little dry powder. And treat anyone who swears a price can't matter the way 1974 treated the Nifty Fifty.
The old investors who survived 1973 had one habit in common: a margin of safety. They simply refused to overpay, even for greatness.
That's the whole game. Not predicting the crash. Just making sure that if it comes, the price you paid gives you room to survive it.
Because the people wiped out in 1974 weren't reckless gamblers. They bought the best, most admired companies in America. They just paid too much.
Lay it end to end and the rhyme is hard to miss.
scenes.title: History rhymes

scenes.narration: History doesn't repeat itself. But, as the line goes, it rhymes. And right now it is rhyming loudly.
And maybe that's the real gift of a forgotten crash. The lessons nobody lived through are the ones a market gets to teach all over again.
You don't have to predict anything to protect yourself. You just have to remember that 1973 happened — and that it started like this.
Nobody knows if the last verse lands the same way. But 1973 whispers one warning: when everyone agrees the price doesn't matter — the price is about to matter a lot.
